content: Agrin is a large proteoglycan that plays a critical role in the development of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) during embryogenesis. Its name is derived from its function in promoting the aggregation of acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) during synaptogenesis. In humans, the AGRN gene encodes this protein. Agrin contains nine domains homologous to protease inhibitors and may also have functions in other tissues and developmental stages. It is a major component of the glomerular basement membrane and may contribute to renal filtration and cell-matrix interactions. When secreted, agrin binds to several receptors on the surface of skeletal muscle. One of these receptors, essential for NMJ formation, is the muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) receptor. MuSK is a receptor tyrosine kinase, meaning it initiates cellular signaling by phosphorylating specific tyrosine residues on itself and on proteins that interact with its cytoplasmic domain. In addition to MuSK, agrin also binds to other muscle surface proteins, such as dystroglycan and laminin, which are necessary for stabilizing the NMJ. The requirement for agrin and MuSK in NMJ formation has been demonstrated through knockout mouse studies. Mice lacking either protein fail to form a functional NMJ. Other proteins are also involved in maintaining NMJ integrity. For instance, MuSK interacts with a protein called Dishevelled (Dvl), part of the Wnt signaling pathway. Dvl is required for MuSK-mediated clustering of AChRs, as inhibiting Dvl prevents this clustering. The nerve secretes agrin, which leads to the phosphorylation of the MuSK receptor. MuSK then recruits casein kinase 2, which is necessary for AChR clustering. A protein called rapsyn is subsequently recruited to the primary MuSK scaffold, facilitating further clustering of AChRs. This process is referred to as the formation of a secondary scaffold. Another protein, Dok-7, is also required for the secondary scaffold's formation. Dok-7 is recruited after MuSK phosphorylation but before AChR clustering. Agrin's primary structure contains three potential heparan sulfate (HS) attachment sites, though only two are thought to carry HS chains when the protein is expressed. Studies have shown that at least two HS attachment sites are necessary for agrin's function. Agrin fragments can induce AChR aggregation and MuSK phosphorylation, but splicing variants that lack these functions fail to trigger phosphorylation. The G3 domain of agrin is highly adaptable, allowing it to selectively bind different partners for optimal interaction. Covalently linked HS glycosaminoglycans on agrin play a role in AChR clustering. Disruption of HS formation, such as by adding chlorate to skeletal muscle cell cultures, reduces the frequency of spontaneous AChR clustering. It is possible that components of the secondary scaffold interact not only with the agrin protein core but also with its HS side chains. Additionally, agrin-linked HS at the glomerular or alveolar basement membrane may play a role in retaining anionic macromolecules within the vasculature.
